import attr


def test_pre_init_with_kw_only_default_field():
    """
    Regression test for: using a __attrs_pre_init__ hook together with a
    keyword-only field that has a default value used to raise a SyntaxError
    while compiling the generated __init__ source (the generated code ended
    up with a malformed, duplicated parameter default assignment like
    ``default=kw_and_default=attr_dict[...].default``).

    Class creation should succeed normally, and the pre-init hook should
    receive the field's default value just like it does without kw_only.
    """
    seen = {}

    @attr.define
    class Foo:
        kw_and_default: int = attr.field(kw_only=True, default=3)

        def __attrs_pre_init__(self, *, kw_and_default):
            seen["value"] = kw_and_default

    # Class creation must not raise (it used to raise SyntaxError here).
    Foo()

    # The pre-init hook must have received the field's default value.
    assert seen["value"] == 3

cases.test_source:
"""
Regression test for: converter lists combined with the default
(implied) on_setattr behaviour of ``attr.define``.

When a field is declared with a *list* of converters
(``attr.field(converter=[int])``), ``attrs`` wraps them with
``attr._make.pipe``, which turns the converter into an
``attrs.Converter`` instance (``takes_self=True, takes_field=True``)
so that it can be invoked correctly from the generated ``__init__``.

However, ``attrs.setters.convert`` -- which is part of the default
``on_setattr`` pipeline that ``attr.define`` installs automatically --
just does ``attrib.converter(new_value)``.  This works fine for plain
callables, but ``Converter`` objects are not callable, so re-assigning
the attribute after construction blows up (or otherwise fails to
apply the converter), instead of behaving exactly like construction
does.

This test pins down the expected behaviour described in the bug
report: setting the attribute after construction must run through the
same converter pipeline as construction and produce a correctly
converted value.
"""

import attr


def test_list_converter_reruns_on_setattr():
    @attr.define
    class C:
        x = attr.field(converter=[int])

    c = C("1")
    assert c.x == 1

    # Re-assigning the attribute should convert the new value the same
    # way construction did.
    c.x = "2"
    assert c.x == 2
    assert isinstance(c.x, int)


def test_list_converter_on_setattr_multiple_reassignments():
    @attr.define
    class C:
        x = attr.field(converter=[str, int])

    c = C(1)
    assert c.x == 1

    c.x = 5
    assert c.x == 5
    assert isinstance(c.x, int)

    c.x = 42
    assert c.x == 42
    assert isinstance(c.x, int)

"""
Regression test for: converter lists combined with the default
(implied) on_setattr behaviour of ``attr.define``.

When a field is declared with a *list* of converters
(``attr.field(converter=[int])``), ``attrs`` wraps them with
``attr._make.pipe``, which turns the converter into an
``attrs.Converter`` instance (``takes_self=True, takes_field=True``)
so that it can be invoked correctly from the generated ``__init__``.

However, ``attrs.setters.convert`` -- which is part of the default
``on_setattr`` pipeline that ``attr.define`` installs automatically --
just does ``attrib.converter(new_value)``.  This works fine for plain
callables, but ``Converter`` objects are not callable, so re-assigning
the attribute after construction blows up (or otherwise fails to
apply the converter), instead of behaving exactly like construction
does.

This test pins down the expected behaviour described in the bug
report: setting the attribute after construction must run through the
same converter pipeline as construction and produce a correctly
converted value.
"""

import attr


def test_list_converter_reruns_on_setattr():
    @attr.define
    class C:
        x = attr.field(converter=[int])

    c = C("1")
    assert c.x == 1

    # Re-assigning the attribute should convert the new value the same
    # way construction did.
    c.x = "2"
    assert c.x == 2
    assert isinstance(c.x, int)


def test_list_converter_on_setattr_multiple_reassignments():
    @attr.define
    class C:
        x = attr.field(converter=[str, int])

    c = C(1)
    assert c.x == 1

    c.x = 5
    assert c.x == 5
    assert isinstance(c.x, int)

    c.x = 42
    assert c.x == 42
    assert isinstance(c.x, int)

cases.rationale: The bug report states that with attr.define (which implies on_setattr running validators/converters), a list-based converter (e.g. converter=[int]) works correctly at construction time but fails to behave the same way when the attribute is reassigned afterwards. Investigation of src/attr/_make.py shows that a converter list is wrapped via pipe(*converters), which returns an attrs.Converter instance (with takes_self=True, takes_field=True) so the compiled __init__/slot __setattr__ can call it properly via Converter._fmt_converter_call. However, attrs.setters.convert (used by the default on_setattr pipeline installed by attr.define) naively does `attrib.converter(new_value)`, and Converter instances are not actually callable (the class declares a "__call__" slot but never defines/assigns a __call__ method), so this raises AttributeError: 'Converter' object has no attribute '__call__' when re-assigning the attribute post-construction. I verified with run_test that the reproduction from the bug report currently fails with exactly this AttributeError on the buggy code. The submitted test asserts the CORRECT expected behavior (that reassignment converts the value the same way construction does, producing an int), which will pass once Converter is made properly callable / setters.convert is fixed to correctly invoke Converter instances, and currently fails on the buggy code.

import typing

import attr
from attr._make import _is_class_var


def test_is_class_var_with_forward_ref():
    """
    _is_class_var should recognize typing.ForwardRef objects that
    represent a ClassVar annotation, not just strings/resolved types.

    On newer Pythons (e.g. 3.14), annotations may be represented lazily
    as ForwardRef objects rather than the resolved typing.ClassVar type
    or a plain string, and attrs needs to detect those too.
    """
    ref = typing.ForwardRef("ClassVar[str]")
    assert _is_class_var(ref)


def test_auto_attribs_strips_classvar_forward_ref():
    """
    Regression test for: attr.s(auto_attribs=True) no longer stripping
    out ClassVar attributes when the annotation ends up being a
    typing.ForwardRef instance (as happens with newer annotation
    evaluation semantics), instead of the resolved typing.ClassVar
    object or a plain string.

    cls_var should be recognized as a ClassVar and therefore NOT show up
    as an attrs field, matching the behavior for resolved ClassVar
    annotations and plain string annotations.
    """

    @attr.s(auto_attribs=True)
    class C:
        cls_var: typing.ForwardRef("typing.ClassVar[str]") = "cls_value"
        value: int = 1

    fields = attr.fields_dict(C)

    assert "cls_var" not in fields
    assert list(fields) == ["value"]

    # The class-level attribute is left alone, and only `value` is a
    # real attrs-managed attribute participating in __init__.
    c = C(2)
    assert c.value == 2
    assert C.cls_var == "cls_value"

The bug report states that on Python 3.14, attr.s(auto_attribs=True) fails to strip ClassVar-annotated attributes when the annotation is represented as a typing.ForwardRef (lazy/unresolved) rather than the resolved typing.ClassVar object or a plain string. The submitted test file has two parts:
1. A focused unit test calling `_is_class_var` directly with a `typing.ForwardRef("ClassVar[str]")` instance, asserting it is correctly identified as a ClassVar (this is the most direct reproduction of the reported defect, independent of how Python's annotation lazy-evaluation machinery constructs ForwardRefs internally).
2. An integration-level test building a real `attr.s(auto_attribs=True)` class where a field's annotation object is a `typing.ForwardRef`, verifying that `attr.fields_dict` excludes `cls_var`, that only `value` becomes a real attrs field, and that constructing the class only requires the non-ClassVar attribute.

I verified both tests fail against the current (buggy) code with genuine assertion failures (not import/attribute errors), confirming they exercise the exact reported behavior. Once `_is_class_var` is fixed to also recognize forward-referenced ClassVar annotations (e.g., by inspecting `__forward_arg__`), both assertions will hold and the tests will pass.

import pytest
import attrs
from contextlib import contextmanager
from attr.exceptions import FrozenInstanceError


@attrs.frozen
class MyException(Exception):
    pass


@contextmanager
def do_nothing():
    yield


def test_frozen_exception_traceback_reassignment_in_context_manager():
    """
    Regression test for: frozen exception classes made with attrs blew up
    (raised FrozenInstanceError) as soon as Python tried to attach/reassign
    a traceback to them (e.g. via contextlib.contextmanager based context
    managers, or manual ``e.__traceback__ = e.__traceback__``).

    Setting __traceback__ is normal exception machinery, not user code
    mutating frozen fields, so it must be allowed to succeed.
    """
    try:
        with do_nothing():
            raise MyException()
    except MyException as e:
        caught = e
    else:
        pytest.fail("MyException was not raised/caught")

    # The context manager's __exit__ already reassigned __traceback__
    # internally (contextlib does `exc.__traceback__ = traceback`), so if
    # we got here without a FrozenInstanceError being raised, that part of
    # the bug is already fixed. Now also exercise the manual re-assignment
    # from the bug report explicitly.
    caught.__traceback__ = caught.__traceback__

    assert caught.__traceback__ is not None


def test_frozen_exception_traceback_manual_reassignment_does_not_raise():
    """
    Directly reproduces the manual reassignment scenario from the bug
    report: assigning an exception's own __traceback__ back to itself
    must not raise FrozenInstanceError for a frozen attrs exception.
    """
    try:
        raise MyException()
    except MyException as e:
        try:
            e.__traceback__ = e.__traceback__
        except FrozenInstanceError:
            pytest.fail(
                "Reassigning __traceback__ on a frozen attrs exception "
                "raised FrozenInstanceError, but it should be allowed."
            )

import attr


def test_old_pickle_tuple_state_restores_all_attributes():
    """
    Regression test for: unpickling old pickle data of a slotted, frozen
    attrs class fails to restore all attributes.

    Older attrs versions serialized instance state for slotted classes as a
    plain tuple of attribute values (in definition order), whereas current
    attrs uses a dict keyed by attribute name. When __setstate__ is handed
    such a legacy tuple, it must still populate every attribute instead of
    silently leaving the instance partially (or entirely) uninitialized.
    """

    @attr.s(slots=True, frozen=True)
    class A:
        x = attr.ib()
        b = attr.ib()
        c = attr.ib()

    a = A(1, 2, 3)

    # Simulate the effect of unpickling data produced by an OLDER attrs
    # version: object.__new__ constructs a bare, uninitialized instance and
    # then pickle calls __setstate__ with the legacy tuple-shaped state
    # (matching the attribute definition order: x, b, c).
    restored = A.__new__(A)
    restored.__setstate__((1, 2, 3))

    # All three attributes must have been restored from the legacy state...
    assert restored.x == 1
    assert restored.b == 2
    assert restored.c == 3

    # ...and the restored object must be usable and compare equal to a
    # freshly constructed, equivalent instance (this used to raise
    # AttributeError instead of returning True).
    assert restored == a

import attr


def test_old_pickle_tuple_state_restores_all_attributes():
    """
    Regression test for: unpickling old pickle data of a slotted, frozen
    attrs class fails to restore all attributes.

    Older attrs versions serialized instance state for slotted classes as a
    plain tuple of attribute values (in definition order), whereas current
    attrs uses a dict keyed by attribute name. When __setstate__ is handed
    such a legacy tuple, it must still populate every attribute instead of
    silently leaving the instance partially (or entirely) uninitialized.
    """

    @attr.s(slots=True, frozen=True)
    class A:
        x = attr.ib()
        b = attr.ib()
        c = attr.ib()

    a = A(1, 2, 3)

    # Simulate the effect of unpickling data produced by an OLDER attrs
    # version: object.__new__ constructs a bare, uninitialized instance and
    # then pickle calls __setstate__ with the legacy tuple-shaped state
    # (matching the attribute definition order: x, b, c).
    restored = A.__new__(A)
    restored.__setstate__((1, 2, 3))

    # All three attributes must have been restored from the legacy state...
    assert restored.x == 1
    assert restored.b == 2
    assert restored.c == 3

    # ...and the restored object must be usable and compare equal to a
    # freshly constructed, equivalent instance (this used to raise
    # AttributeError instead of returning True).
    assert restored == a

cases.rationale: The bug: attrs' generated __setstate__ for slotted classes (slots_setstate in _make.py) assumes the pickled state is a dict ({name: value}) and does `if name in state: __bound_setattr(name, state[name])`. Older attrs versions serialized slotted-class state as a plain tuple of values in attribute-definition order, so pickle data created with those versions still calls __setstate__ with a tuple. When state is a tuple, `name in state` checks membership of a string in a tuple of values, which is always False, so no attributes get set at all, leaving the restored object completely uninitialized. Accessing any attribute (e.g. during __eq__) then raises AttributeError, matching the report. The fix must special-case tuple/list state (or otherwise support legacy formats) and restore attributes positionally. This test directly exercises A.__new__(A).__setstate__((1, 2, 3)) - reproducing the legacy pickle payload's call pattern - and asserts all three attributes are correctly restored and that the restored instance compares equal to a freshly built equivalent instance. It fails on the current buggy implementation (AttributeError: 'A' object has no attribute 'x') and should pass once __setstate__ correctly handles legacy tuple-based state.

import inspect

from attr._cmp import cmp_using


def test_ne_docstring_has_no_incidental_indentation():
    """
    Regression test for: "the docstring of the generated 'not equal'
    method doesn't match between Python versions".

    ``cmp_using()`` builds classes whose ``__ne__`` method keeps the raw,
    literal docstring written inside ``attr._make._make_ne``. Because that
    docstring is a multi-line triple-quoted string nested inside a function
    body, its continuation line inherits the *source* indentation. Whether
    that incidental indentation survives into ``__doc__`` depends on how the
    interpreter's compiler stores docstrings, which changed between Python
    versions (e.g. 3.12 keeps the leading spaces on continuation lines,
    3.13 strips them). This makes ``__ne__.__doc__`` differ across
    versions for the exact same source code, which breaks anything relying
    on exact docstring text (e.g. snapshot tests).

    The generated docstring should be stable and not depend on this
    incidental, version-specific compiler behavior: once meaningless
    surrounding whitespace is stripped, its content must already match the
    canonical/"cleaned" form produced by ``inspect.cleandoc``, on every
    supported Python version.
    """
    C = cmp_using(eq=lambda a, b: a == b)
    doc = C.__ne__.__doc__

    assert doc is not None

    # inspect.cleandoc() normalizes indentation the same way regardless of
    # the interpreter's docstring-compilation quirks. If the generated
    # docstring is already free of incidental, version-dependent
    # indentation on its continuation lines, stripping the surrounding
    # whitespace should already match what cleandoc() would produce.
    assert doc.strip() == inspect.cleandoc(doc)

    # Pin down the actual expected wording too, so a change that alters
    # the message itself (rather than just its indentation) is still
    # caught.
    assert doc.strip() == (
        "Check equality and either forward a NotImplemented or\n"
        "return the result negated."
    ) or doc.strip() == (
        "Check equality and either forward a NotImplemented or "
        "return the result negated."

import inspect

from attr._cmp import cmp_using


def test_ne_docstring_has_no_incidental_indentation():
    """
    Regression test for: "the docstring of the generated 'not equal'
    method doesn't match between Python versions".

    ``cmp_using()`` builds classes whose ``__ne__`` method keeps the raw,
    literal docstring written inside ``attr._make._make_ne``. Because that
    docstring is a multi-line triple-quoted string nested inside a function
    body, its continuation line inherits the *source* indentation. Whether
    that incidental indentation survives into ``__doc__`` depends on how the
    interpreter's compiler stores docstrings, which changed between Python
    versions (e.g. 3.12 keeps the leading spaces on continuation lines,
    3.13 strips them). This makes ``__ne__.__doc__`` differ across
    versions for the exact same source code, which breaks anything relying
    on exact docstring text (e.g. snapshot tests).

    The generated docstring should be stable and not depend on this
    incidental, version-specific compiler behavior: once meaningless
    surrounding whitespace is stripped, its content must already match the
    canonical/"cleaned" form produced by ``inspect.cleandoc``, on every
    supported Python version.
    """
    C = cmp_using(eq=lambda a, b: a == b)
    doc = C.__ne__.__doc__

    assert doc is not None

    # inspect.cleandoc() normalizes indentation the same way regardless of
    # the interpreter's docstring-compilation quirks. If the generated
    # docstring is already free of incidental, version-dependent
    # indentation on its continuation lines, stripping the surrounding
    # whitespace should already match what cleandoc() would produce.
    assert doc.strip() == inspect.cleandoc(doc)

    # Pin down the actual expected wording too, so a change that alters
    # the message itself (rather than just its indentation) is still
    # caught.
    assert doc.strip() == (

        "return the result negated."

from boltons.strutils import singularize


def test_double_s_singular_words_unchanged():
    # Words that are already singular but end in a double 's' should
    # pass through unchanged, not have a trailing 's' stripped off.
    assert singularize('glass') == 'glass'
    assert singularize('boss') == 'boss'
    assert singularize('kiss') == 'kiss'
    assert singularize('class') == 'class'
    assert singularize('address') == 'address'


def test_plural_sses_still_works():
    # Actual plurals ending in 'sses' should still singularize correctly.
    assert singularize('glasses') == 'glass'


def test_idempotency():
    # Running singularize on its own output should be a no-op once the
    # word is already singular.
    assert singularize(singularize('Glasses')) == 'Glass'

Tracing boltons/strutils.py's singularize(): for such words, none of the special-case branches ('ies' or 'es' with preceding 's', i.e. 'sses') match because the word ends in plain 'ss' not 'es', so it falls through to the generic `singular = word[:-1]` branch, incorrectly stripping the final 's'. import shutil
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

from boltons import fileutils


def test_atomic_saver_accepts_pathlib_path():
    """AtomicSaver should accept os.PathLike destinations (e.g. pathlib.Path),
    not just plain strings, just like open() and the rest of the os/pathlib
    ecosystem. Previously this raised:
        TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'PosixPath' and 'str'
    because the constructor did `dest_path + '.part'` on the raw, un-stringified
    dest_path argument.
    """
    tmpdir = tempfile.mkdtemp()
    try:
        dest = Path(tmpdir) / 'output.bin'
        with fileutils.AtomicSaver(dest) as f:
            f.write(b'hello')
        assert dest.exists()
        assert dest.read_bytes() == b'hello'
    finally:
        shutil.rmtree(tmpdir, ignore_errors=True)

import shutil
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

from boltons import fileutils


def test_atomic_saver_accepts_pathlib_path():
    """AtomicSaver should accept os.PathLike destinations (e.g. pathlib.Path),
    not just plain strings, just like open() and the rest of the os/pathlib
    ecosystem. Previously this raised:
        TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'PosixPath' and 'str'
    because the constructor did `dest_path + '.part'` on the raw, un-stringified
    dest_path argument.
    """
    tmpdir = tempfile.mkdtemp()
    try:
        dest = Path(tmpdir) / 'output.bin'
        with fileutils.AtomicSaver(dest) as f:
            f.write(b'hello')
        assert dest.exists()
        assert dest.read_bytes() == b'hello'
    finally:
        shutil.rmtree(tmpdir, ignore_errors=True)

def test_short_row_no_headers_renders_without_header_row():
    # Table([[], [1]]) previously raised IndexError. With no headers
    # supplied, to_text() should just render the (padded) data rows,
    # without a header row.
    t = Table([[], [1]])
    result = t.to_text()
    lines = result.split('\n')
    # No headers were given, so there should be no header/separator
    # lines -- just the two data rows.
    assert len(lines) == 2
    assert lines[0].strip() == 'None'
    assert lines[1].strip() == '1'


def test_headers_shorter_than_row_width_are_padded():
    # Table constructed with no headers, then headers assigned
    # afterwards that are shorter than the row width, previously
    # raised IndexError. Headers should be padded out (with None,
    # rendered like a normal data cell) to match the row width.

    t.headers = ['a']

    lines = result.split('\n')

from boltons.tableutils import Table


def test_empty_table_renders_empty_string():
    # Table([[]]) should not raise, and should render to an empty string.
    t = Table([[]])
    assert t.to_text() == ''


def test_short_row_no_headers_renders_without_header_row():
    # Table([[], [1]]) previously raised IndexError. With no headers
    # supplied, to_text() should just render the (padded) data rows,
    # without a header row.
    t = Table([[], [1]])
    result = t.to_text()
    lines = result.split('\n')
    # No headers were given, so there should be no header/separator
    # lines -- just the two data rows.
    assert len(lines) == 2
    assert lines[0].strip() == 'None'
    assert lines[1].strip() == '1'


def test_headers_shorter_than_row_width_are_padded():
    # Table constructed with no headers, then headers assigned
    # afterwards that are shorter than the row width, previously
    # raised IndexError. Headers should be padded out (with None,
    # rendered like a normal data cell) to match the row width.
    t = Table([[1, 2]], headers=[])
    t.headers = ['a']
    result = t.to_text()
    lines = result.split('\n')
    # header row + separator row + 1 data row
    assert len(lines) == 3
    header_cells = [c.strip() for c in lines[0].split('|')]
    assert header_cells[0] == 'a'
    assert header_cells[1] == 'None'
    data_cells = [c.strip() for c in lines[2].split('|')]
    assert data_cells == ['1', '2']


def test_none_header_cell_renders_like_none_data_cell():
    # When headers contain None (e.g. guessed from the first data row),
    # to_text() previously raised AttributeError trying to call
    # .center() on None directly. It should instead render the header
    # the same way a None data cell renders (i.e. as the text 'None').
    t = Table([[None, 'b'], [1, 2]])
    result = t.to_text()
    lines = result.split('\n')
    assert len(lines) == 3
    header_cells = [c.strip() for c in lines[0].split('|')]
    assert header_cells[0] == 'None'
    assert header_cells[1] == 'b'
    data_cells = [c.strip() for c in lines[2].split('|')]
    assert data_cells == ['1', '2']

This test builds an OMD with a key ('a') that has two values, performs both a shallow copy and a deep copy, and asserts that (1) the copies compare equal to the original OMD, and (2) getlist('a') returns all originally inserted values ([1, 2]) rather than just the last one ([2]). import io
import json
import threading

from boltons.jsonutils import JSONLIterator


def _run_with_timeout(target, timeout=5.0):
    """Run target() in a background thread; return (finished, result_dict).

    result_dict has 'value' on success or 'exc' if target() raised.
    Using a thread (instead of calling target() directly) means that even
    if JSONLIterator hangs forever, this test terminates promptly after
    `timeout` seconds instead of blocking the whole test run.
    """
    result = {}

    def wrapper():
        try:
            result['value'] = target()
        except Exception as e:
            result['exc'] = e

    t = threading.Thread(target=wrapper, daemon=True)
    t.start()
    t.join(timeout)
    finished = not t.is_alive()
    return finished, result


def test_jsonl_iterator_no_trailing_newline_rel_seek_does_not_hang():
    # Regression test for: JSONLIterator hangs forever when a rel_seek
    # value lands inside the last line of a file that doesn't end with a
    # newline (see bug report repro).
    data = '{"1": 1}\n{"2": 2}'

    def go():
        f = io.StringIO(data)
        it = JSONLIterator(f, rel_seek=0.9)
        return list(it)

    finished, result = _run_with_timeout(go, timeout=5.0)
    assert finished, (
        "JSONLIterator hung when rel_seek landed inside the final line "
        "of a file without a trailing newline"
    )
    # A raised error would also be an acceptable outcome per the bug report,
    # but if it completed normally the result should at least be a usable
    # list (not garbage/partial state from a broken seek).
    if 'exc' not in result:
        assert isinstance(result['value'], list)


def test_jsonl_iterator_negative_rel_seek_does_not_hang_and_seeks_from_end():
    # Regression test for: a negative rel_seek value causes JSONLIterator to
    # seek past the end of the file and spin forever, instead of seeking
    # relative to the end of the file the way negative indices normally do
    # (per the bug report, rel_seek=-0.5 should behave like
    # rel_seek == 1.0 + (-0.5) == 0.5).
    data = '\n'.join(json.dumps({'n': i}) for i in range(20)) + '\n'

    def go_negative():
        f = io.StringIO(data)
        it = JSONLIterator(f, rel_seek=-0.5)
        return list(it)

    def go_positive():
        f = io.StringIO(data)
        it = JSONLIterator(f, rel_seek=0.5)
        return list(it)

    finished_neg, result_neg = _run_with_timeout(go_negative, timeout=5.0)
    assert finished_neg, (
        "JSONLIterator hung on a negative rel_seek value instead of "
        "seeking relative to the end of the file"
    )
    assert 'exc' not in result_neg, (
        "unexpected exception for rel_seek=-0.5: %r" % result_neg.get('exc')
    )

    finished_pos, result_pos = _run_with_timeout(go_positive, timeout=5.0)
    assert finished_pos
    assert 'exc' not in result_pos

    # Negative rel_seek of -0.5 should behave like seeking from the end,
    # equivalent to positive rel_seek of 1.0 + (-0.5) == 0.5
    assert result_neg['value'] == result_pos['value']
    assert len(result_neg['value']) > 0

cases.rationale:
The bug report describes JSONLIterator hanging forever (never returning, never raising) in two related scenarios caused by boltons/jsonutils.py's rel_seek handling: (1) when rel_seek lands inside the final line of a file lacking a trailing newline, `_align_to_newline`'s `while '\n' not in cur` loop spins forever because `fo.read(bsize)` returns '' at EOF forever; (2) for negative rel_seek, the code computes `rel_seek = 1.0 - rel_seek` instead of `1.0 + rel_seek`, pushing the target seek position past EOF, which triggers the same infinite loop in `_align_to_newline`.

Because the buggy behavior is an infinite loop (not an exception), the test can't call the buggy code directly without risking hanging the test run forever. Each test therefore runs the iterator construction/consumption in a daemon thread and joins with a bounded timeout, then asserts the thread actually finished — this fails on the buggy code (thread is still alive after the timeout, confirmed by run_test output) and will pass on a fix that resolves the hang.

The second test additionally pins down the *correct* expected behavior for negative rel_seek explicitly named in the report ("I expected negative values to seek from the end... instead it seeks past the end and spins"): rel_seek=-0.5 should produce the same result as rel_seek=0.5 (i.e., the fix should use `1.0 + rel_seek`), not just avoid hanging.

Ran via run_test against the current buggy code: both tests fail with the intended "hung" AssertionError (not an ImportError/TypeError from a wrong API guess), confirming they exercise the real reported defect.

    assert 1 not in cache
    assert 2 not in cache

from cachetools import TLRUCache


def ttu(_k, value, t):
    return t + value


def test_overwrite_with_already_expired_value_drops_key():
    """
    Regression test for: TLRUCache overwriting an existing key with a value
    that is already expired at insertion time keeps the old value instead
    of dropping the key.

    With ttu(key, value, t) = t + value, setting cache[1] = 0 at time 0
    computes expires = 0, so the new entry is expired the instant it is
    set (not (time < expires) is True). The cache should therefore not
    keep serving the *old* value for key 1 -- the key should be dropped
    (evicted) rather than silently continuing to return the previous,
    stale value as if nothing happened.
    """
    cache = TLRUCache(maxsize=2, ttu=ttu, timer=lambda: 0)

    cache[1] = 5
    assert cache[1] == 5
    assert 1 in cache
    assert len(cache) == 1

    # Overwrite key 1 with a value that is already expired at insertion time.
    cache[1] = 0

    # The key must not silently keep serving the old value.
    assert 1 not in cache
    assert len(cache) == 0

    try:
        value = cache[1]
    except KeyError:
        pass
    else:
        raise AssertionError(
            "expected KeyError for expired key 1, got stale value %r" % (value,)
        )

import itertools
import more_itertools as mi


def test_nth_product_with_iterators_and_repeat():
    """
    Regression test for: nth_product/product_index give wrong results (or
    crash) when the iterables passed in are one-shot iterators combined
    with `repeat`, instead of reusable sequences like strings/lists.

    The result should be identical whether we pass reusable sequences or
    iterators over the same sequences.
    """
    index = 123
    repeat = 2
    letters = ('AB', 'CD', 'EFG')

    # Ground truth via itertools.product: each of the `repeat` copies of
    # each iterable is independently iterable.
    materialized = [list(s) for s in letters] * repeat
    expected = list(itertools.product(*materialized))[index]

    # Works correctly for plain sequences (per the bug report).
    result_strs = mi.nth_product(index, *letters, repeat=repeat)
    assert result_strs == expected

    # Should give the same result when passing one-shot iterators.
    result_iters = mi.nth_product(
        index, *(iter(s) for s in letters), repeat=repeat
    )
    assert result_iters == expected


def test_product_index_with_iterators_and_repeat():
    """
    Regression test for: product_index gives wrong results (or crashes)
    when the iterables passed in are one-shot iterators combined with
    `repeat`, instead of reusable sequences like strings/lists.
    """
    repeat = 2
    letters = ('AB', 'CD', 'EFG')
    target = ('A', 'D', 'G', 'B', 'C', 'E')

cases.rationale:
The bug is in more_itertools/more.py's nth_product and product_index: both do `iterables * repeat` on the raw *iterables* tuple before materializing each into a tuple via `map(tuple, ...)`. When iterables are reusable sequences (str/list), Python's sequence multiplication makes independent references that each iterate fine. But when iterables are one-shot iterators, `iterables * repeat` just repeats references to the SAME iterator objects; the first `tuple(iterator)` call exhausts each iterator, so every subsequent occurrence of that same iterator in the repeated tuple materializes to an empty tuple. This corrupts the `pools`/`ns` computation, producing wrong results or spurious IndexError/ValueError.

The fix should materialize/repeat each iterable's *values* (not the iterator object) `repeat` times, so that passing `iter('AB')` behaves identically to passing `'AB'`.

This test reproduces the exact scenario from the bug report (nth_product and product_index called with `iter(...)` iterables and `repeat=2`), computes the objectively correct expected values using `itertools.product` (which correctly handles repeat by using materialized lists), and asserts that both the string-based call (already correct, per the report) and the iterator-based call return that same, correct result.

Confirmed via run_test: on the current buggy code, the iterator-based calls raise IndexError / ValueError instead of returning the correct tuple/index, so the test fails on the buggy code. Once the fix correctly repeats materialized values instead of iterator references, both calls will return the same correct result and the test will pass.

import more_itertools as mi


def test_random_product_with_iterators_and_repeat():
    """
    Regression test for: random_product() with repeat > 1 raises IndexError
    when passed iterators (as opposed to lists/sequences).

    The bug: `pools = tuple(map(tuple, iterables * repeat))` repeats the
    *iterable objects* themselves. For sequences like lists this is fine
    because each one can be iterated over multiple times, but for iterators
    the same (now-exhausted) iterator object appears multiple times in the
    repeated tuple, so every occurrence after the first turns into an empty
    pool, causing `random.choice` to raise IndexError.

    The fix should consume each iterable once into a pool and reuse that
    pool for each repetition, so passing iterators behaves the same as
    passing lists.
    """
    nums = [1, 2, 3]
    lets = ['a', 'b', 'c']

    # Should not raise, and should behave equivalently to passing lists.
    result = mi.random_product(iter(nums), iter(lets), repeat=5)

    assert len(result) == 2 * 5
    # Even positions are drawn from `nums`, odd positions from `lets`,
    # mirroring itertools.product(*iterables, repeat=repeat) ordering.
    for i, value in enumerate(result):
        if i % 2 == 0:
            assert value in nums
        else:
            assert value in lets

import pytest
import more_itertools as mi


def test_tail_negative_n_sized_iterable_raises():
    """
    Regression test: tail(n, iterable) with a negative n should raise a
    ValueError regardless of whether the iterable is sized (has a __len__,
    e.g. a string or list) or unsized (e.g. a generator).

    Previously, the sized code path in `tail` used
    `islice(iterable, max(0, size - n), None)` which, for negative n,
    silently computed a start index of `size - n` (larger than size) and
    returned an empty iterator instead of raising -- inconsistent with the
    unsized path which raises ValueError via deque(maxlen=n) for negative n.
    """
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        list(mi.tail(-1, 'ABCDEFG'))

    # Sanity check: sized and unsized code paths should now agree
    # (unsized path already raises ValueError for negative n).
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        list(mi.tail(-1, iter('ABCDEFG')))

from fractions import Fraction

import more_itertools as mi


def test_running_min_stable_type_on_ties():
    # Values are numerically equal but of different types. running_min
    # should behave like the builtin `min`, which is stable and returns
    # the first argument when values compare equal, so the *type* of the
    # returned element for each window should match what plain `min`
    # would produce over the same window.
    data = [0, 0.0, Fraction(0)]
    result_types = list(map(type, mi.running_min(data, maxlen=2)))
    expected_types = [
        type(min(data[0:1])),
        type(min(data[0:2])),
        type(min(data[1:3])),
    ]
    assert result_types == expected_types

    # Same issue as running_min, but for running_max.

    result_types = list(map(type, mi.running_max(data, maxlen=2)))
    expected_types = [
        type(max(data[0:1])),
        type(max(data[0:2])),
        type(max(data[1:3])),
    ]
    assert result_types == expected_types

from fractions import Fraction

import more_itertools as mi


def test_running_min_stable_type_on_ties():
    # Values are numerically equal but of different types. running_min
    # should behave like the builtin `min`, which is stable and returns
    # the first argument when values compare equal, so the *type* of the
    # returned element for each window should match what plain `min`
    # would produce over the same window.
    data = [0, 0.0, Fraction(0)]
    result_types = list(map(type, mi.running_min(data, maxlen=2)))
    expected_types = [
        type(min(data[0:1])),
        type(min(data[0:2])),
        type(min(data[1:3])),
    ]
    assert result_types == expected_types


def test_running_max_stable_type_on_ties():
    # Same issue as running_min, but for running_max.
    data = [0, 0.0, Fraction(0)]
    result_types = list(map(type, mi.running_max(data, maxlen=2)))
    expected_types = [
        type(max(data[0:1])),
        type(max(data[0:2])),
        type(max(data[1:3])),
    ]
    assert result_types == expected_types

def test_dynamic_invalid_field_error_names_specific_field():
    """
    When `dynamic` contains a disallowed field (name/version/metadata-version)
    alongside other dynamic fields, the InvalidMetadata error message should

def test_wildcard_equal_with_epoch_and_extra_trailing_zero_segments():
    # ``2!1.0.0`` has the same epoch (2) as the specifier, and its release
    # segment ``1.0.0`` is equivalent to ``1.0.0.0`` once trailing zeros are
    # considered equal, so it should match the ``==2!1.0.0.0.*`` wildcard
    # prefix specifier. This is the case reported as broken: once the
    # wildcard specifier has more trailing-zero release segments than a
    # plain "X.Y" shape, the epoch-aware padding logic in
    # Specifier._compare_equal / _pad_version mishandles the epoch prefix
    # (e.g. "2!1") and fails to zero-pad the shorter release segment
    # correctly, causing this legitimate match to be rejected.
    assert SpecifierSet("==2!1.0.0.0.*").contains("2!1.0.0") is True

cases.rationale: The bug report concerns Specifier._compare_equal's wildcard (".*") handling combined with _pad_version when an epoch is present in either the prospective version or the specifier, especially once the specifier has more release segments than a plain "X.Y" shape (extra trailing zeros). Tracing the buggy implementation: canonicalize_version keeps the epoch as a prefix on the first release token (e.g. "2!1"), so when _version_split splits on ".", the epoch gets fused onto the first numeric segment. _pad_version then uses itertools.takewhile(lambda x: x.isdigit(), ...) to separate the "release segment" for zero-padding purposes; because "2!1" is not a pure digit string, this takewhile immediately returns an empty list whenever an epoch is present, so no zero-padding is inserted for the release numbers. This is harmless when the two version lengths already match, but breaks once the specifier has extra trailing ".0" segments beyond what the prospective version has (i.e. after epoch introduces the mismatch that padding was meant to fix). I confirmed by running against the buggy code that SpecifierSet("==2!1.0.0.0.*").contains("2!1.0.0") returns False, even though 1.0.0 and 1.0.0.0 are equivalent release segments and the epochs match (both 2), so this should be True per the report ("2!1.0.0 should match ==2!1.0.0.0.*"). I also verified the two simpler epoch-mismatch examples from the report (==1.0.0.* vs 2!1.0, and ==2!1.0.0.* vs 1.0) already correctly return False on this checkout, so I included them as non-regressing sanity checks in a separate test but built the core regression assertion around the confirmed-broken case, which fails cleanly with an AssertionError (False is True) on the buggy code and encodes the behavior the report says is correct.

from semver import Version


class MyVersion(Version):
    """A trivial subclass of Version, used to test cross-class comparison."""

    pass


def test_compare_subclass_symmetric():
    """
    Regression test: Version.compare() must be symmetric regardless of
    which side (base class instance or subclass instance) it is called on.

    Previously, `subclass_instance.compare(base_instance)` raised a
    TypeError because compare() checked `isinstance(other, type(self))`
    instead of `isinstance(other, Version)`. This meant that comparing
    a Version with a subclass instance depended on which side was "self".
    """
    a = MyVersion.parse("1.0.0")
    b = Version.parse("1.0.0")

    # This direction already worked before the fix.
    assert b.compare(a) == 0

    # This direction used to raise TypeError; it should behave the same
    # as the other direction and report equal versions.
    assert a.compare(b) == 0

from tabulate import tabulate, SEPARATING_LINE


def test_github_with_separating_line():
    """Regression test: SEPARATING_LINE inside a data row must render as a
    normal divider line even for tablefmt with padding/linebetweenrows
    (e.g. "github"), instead of leaking the internal SEPARATING_LINE
    control character into the output and losing column widths."""
    table = [["spam", 41.9999], SEPARATING_LINE, ["eggs", 451]]
    result = tabulate(table, tablefmt="github")

    expected = "\n".join(
        [
            "|------|----------|",
            "| spam |  41.9999 |",
            "|------|----------|",
            "| eggs | 451      |",
        ]
    )
    assert result == expected

from tabulate import tabulate, SEPARATING_LINE


def test_github_with_separating_line():
    """Regression test: SEPARATING_LINE inside a data row must render as a
    normal divider line even for tablefmt with padding/linebetweenrows
    (e.g. "github"), instead of leaking the internal SEPARATING_LINE
    control character into the output and losing column widths."""
    table = [["spam", 41.9999], SEPARATING_LINE, ["eggs", 451]]
    result = tabulate(table, tablefmt="github")

    expected = "\n".join(
        [
            "|------|----------|",
            "| spam |  41.9999 |",
            "|------|----------|",
            "| eggs | 451      |",
        ]
    )
    assert result == expected

This test reproduces the exact example from the report with tablefmt="github" and asserts the correct expected output (a proper dashed divider line in place of the SEPARATING_LINE marker, with correct column widths preserved) as given in the bug report. On the current buggy code, the row containing the raw SEPARATING_LINE control character gets padded/rendered as a normal data row, producing a broken line like "|  |" with an embedded \x01 character and lost column widths, causing the assertion to fail. Once the code is fixed to also honor SEPARATING_LINE in that code path, the output will match the expected divider-based rendering and the test will pass.

"""Regression test for: tabulate raises when a list of dataclass instances
is mixed with SEPARATING_LINE.

Bug report: using tabulate() with a list of dataclass rows that also
contains tabulate.SEPARATING_LINE raises an AttributeError, because the
dataclass-normalization code path tries to call getattr(row, field_name)
on the SEPARATING_LINE marker itself (which is just the string "\\x01"),
instead of skipping it the way other separating-line-aware code paths do.

Expected behaviour (per the report): tabulate should produce a table with
headers derived from the dataclass fields and a separating line drawn
between the two data rows, exactly as it does for the equivalent
list-of-lists input.
"""

from dataclasses import make_dataclass

from tabulate import tabulate, SEPARATING_LINE


def test_dataclass_rows_with_separating_line():
    Person = make_dataclass("Person", ["name", "age", "height"])
    data = [
        Person("Alice", 23, 169.5),
        SEPARATING_LINE,
        Person("Bob", 27, 175.0),
    ]

    # Should not raise, and should render the same way that an equivalent
    # list-of-lists table (with the same headers and the same separating
    # line placement) renders.
    result = tabulate(data, headers="keys", tablefmt="plain")

    expected = (
        "name      age    height\n"
        "Alice      23     169.5\n"
        "\n"
        "Bob        27     175"
    )
    assert result == expected

is mixed with SEPARATING_LINE.

Bug report: using tabulate() with a list of dataclass rows that also
contains tabulate.SEPARATING_LINE raises an AttributeError, because the
dataclass-normalization code path tries to call getattr(row, field_name)
on the SEPARATING_LINE marker itself (which is just the string "\\x01"),
instead of skipping it the way other separating-line-aware code paths do.

Expected behaviour (per the report): tabulate should produce a table with
headers derived from the dataclass fields and a separating line drawn
between the two data rows, exactly as it does for the equivalent
list-of-lists input.

from tabulate import tabulate, SEPARATING_LINE


def test_dataclass_rows_with_separating_line():
    Person = make_dataclass("Person", ["name", "age", "height"])
    data = [
        Person("Alice", 23, 169.5),
        SEPARATING_LINE,
        Person("Bob", 27, 175.0),
    ]

    # Should not raise, and should render the same way that an equivalent
    # list-of-lists table (with the same headers and the same separating
    # line placement) renders.
    result = tabulate(data, headers="keys", tablefmt="plain")

    )

def test_empty_data_with_maxcolwidths_returns_empty_string():
    """

from tabulate import tabulate


def test_decimal_floatfmt_preserves_precision():
    """Regression test: tabulate should format Decimal values using their own
    precision when floatfmt is applied, not by first converting to float
    (which introduces precision drift / incorrect rounding).

    See bug report: Decimal("99999998999.999980") formatted with floatfmt=".6f"
    should render as "99999998999.999980" (exact value, truncated/rounded to
    6 decimal places from the Decimal itself), not "99999998999.999985" which
    is what you get if the Decimal is first coerced to a float.
    """
    result = tabulate(
        [[Decimal("99999998999.999980"), 1234.5, 1.2345678, "inf"]],
        floatfmt=".6f",
        tablefmt="plain",
    )

    assert "99999998999.999980" in result
    # Sanity: it must NOT have drifted to the float-precision-loss value.
    assert "99999998999.999985" not in result

    # The other columns (float, float, string) should still format normally.
    assert "1234.500000" in result
    assert "1.234568" in result
    assert "inf" in result

from decimal import Decimal
from tabulate import tabulate


def test_decimal_floatfmt_preserves_precision():
    """Regression test: tabulate should format Decimal values using their own
    precision when floatfmt is applied, not by first converting to float
    (which introduces precision drift / incorrect rounding).

    See bug report: Decimal("99999998999.999980") formatted with floatfmt=".6f"
    should render as "99999998999.999980" (exact value, truncated/rounded to
    6 decimal places from the Decimal itself), not "99999998999.999985" which
    is what you get if the Decimal is first coerced to a float.
    """
    result = tabulate(
        [[Decimal("99999998999.999980"), 1234.5, 1.2345678, "inf"]],
        floatfmt=".6f",
        tablefmt="plain",
    )

    # The Decimal must retain its exact digits when formatted to 6 dp.
    assert "99999998999.999980" in result
    # Sanity: it must NOT have drifted to the float-precision-loss value.
    assert "99999998999.999985" not in result

    # The other columns (float, float, string) should still format normally.
    assert "1234.500000" in result
    assert "1.234568" in result
    assert "inf" in result

import pytest
from tabulate import tabulate


def test_maxcolwidths_with_bool_string_and_none_cell():
    """Regression: using maxcolwidths on a table containing a "True"/"False"
    string cell or a None cell should wrap those cells like normal strings
    (bool-like strings as text, None as blank) instead of raising an
    exception in the internal text-wrapping step.
    """
    data = [
        ["First Entry", "True"],
        ["Second Entry", None],
    ]
    headers = ["Title", "When"]

    # Should not raise (previously raised AttributeError/TypeError because
    # the type-detection logic used before wrapping mis-cast "True" to an
    # actual bool object and tried to instantiate NoneType(None) for None).
    result = tabulate(data, headers=headers, tablefmt="grid", maxcolwidths=[7, 5])

    # "True" should appear verbatim as wrapped text, not have crashed the cast.
    assert "True" in result

    # None should be rendered as blank/empty, not as the literal string "None".
    assert "None" not in result

    # The other column's long words should still be wrapped across lines,
    # confirming maxcolwidths wrapping still functions for the whole row.
    assert "First" in result
    assert "Entry" in result
    assert "Second" in result

from tabulate import tabulate


def test_maxcolwidths_with_bool_string_and_none_cell():
    """Regression: using maxcolwidths on a table containing a "True"/"False"
    string cell or a None cell should wrap those cells like normal strings
    (bool-like strings as text, None as blank) instead of raising an
    exception in the internal text-wrapping step.
    """
    data = [
        ["First Entry", "True"],
        ["Second Entry", None],
    ]
    headers = ["Title", "When"]

    # Should not raise (previously raised AttributeError/TypeError because
    # the type-detection logic used before wrapping mis-cast "True" to an
    # actual bool object and tried to instantiate NoneType(None) for None).
    result = tabulate(data, headers=headers, tablefmt="grid", maxcolwidths=[7, 5])

    # "True" should appear verbatim as wrapped text, not have crashed the cast.
    assert "True" in result

    # None should be rendered as blank/empty, not as the literal string "None".
    assert "None" not in result

    # confirming maxcolwidths wrapping still functions for the whole row.
    assert "First" in result
    assert "Entry" in result
    assert "Second" in result

cases.rationale: The bug report states that using maxcolwidths on a table with a "True"/"False" string cell or a None cell raises an exception during the internal text-wrapping step (_wrap_text_to_colwidths / _type), instead of wrapping those cells as plain text. Running the exact repro from the report against the current buggy code confirms it raises AttributeError: 'bool' object has no attribute 'splitlines' (because _type() misclassifies "True" as bool and casts it to an actual bool object before calling .splitlines() on it; a None cell similarly fails because NoneType(None) cannot be instantiated). The test asserts the corrected expected behavior: tabulate() completes without raising, "True" appears verbatim in the rendered output, "None" does not appear as a literal string (it should render as blank), and the other column's text wrapping still works normally. This will fail on the buggy code (exception raised) and pass once the type-detection/casting logic is fixed to treat these values as text for wrapping purposes.
